title: Summer pudding
summary: A dome of juice-soaked low-carb sponge packed with lightly cooked summer berries, pressed overnight.

ingredients.note: melted, plus a little for the tin

steps: Heat the oven to 175 °C (350 °F). Oil a 23 × 33 cm (9 × 13 in) baking tin and line it with parchment.
Whisk the eggs and erythritol until pale and thick, about 3 minutes. Whisk the almond flour, psyllium, baking powder and salt together, then fold them in with the melted coconut oil.
Spread thinly and evenly in the tin and bake 15–18 minutes, until springy and lightly golden. Cool completely; this thin sheet stands in for the white bread of the classic pudding.
Put the berries, erythritol and water in a pan and warm over medium-low heat for 3–4 minutes, just until the juices run and the sweetener dissolves. The fruit should keep its shape. Cool slightly.
Line a 1-litre (1-quart) pudding basin with cling film. Cut a round of sponge for the base and strips for the sides, overlapping them slightly. Brush the sponge generously with the berry juice.
Spoon in the fruit with most of the remaining juice, keeping 3–4 tablespoons back. Cover with a lid of sponge.
Fold the film over, set a saucer on top and weigh it down with a couple of cans. Refrigerate at least 8 hours.
Turn out onto a plate and spoon the reserved juice over any pale patches. Cut into wedges.
tips: Almond sponge is softer than stale white bread; pressing it overnight with a weight is what makes it hold its shape, so do not skip it.

origin.history: Summer pudding is an English dessert of stale white bread soaked in the juice of lightly stewed soft fruit and pressed in a basin. It is often said to have begun as a lighter alternative to pastry puddings for health-conscious diners in the late nineteenth century, and it became a classic of the English summer by the early twentieth. The low-carb sponge here replaces the bread.
